title: Vayechi: crossed hands (Genesis 48:13–20)
hookLine: Jacob crosses his hands to bless the younger grandson first

cards: In plenty of families, the older one gets introduced first. Gets the bigger bedroom, the first car, the photo in the middle. The younger one learns to stand a little to the side.
Now Joseph arranges his two sons in front of their grandfather for a blessing. He's careful. The older boy goes to Jacob's right hand, the hand of the stronger blessing.
The younger goes to his left. Everything in order. Then the old man, nearly blind, does something with his arms.

teach.b: Jacob crosses his hands. His right hand goes onto the head of Ephraim, the younger. His left onto Manasseh, the firstborn.
In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "guiding his hands wittingly." On purpose. Joseph is upset.
He takes his father's hand to move it: not that way, father, this one's the firstborn.

teach.h: I KNOW IT, MY SON, I KNOW IT.
teach.b: And Jacob says: "I know it, my son, I know it." He doesn't stop. The younger one, he says, will be greater.
But the older one, too, will become a people, and he too will be great.
Then Jacob says: from now on, when the people of Israel bless their children, they'll say, "God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." And they do.
On Friday nights, in many Jewish homes, parents place their hands on their sons' heads and say exactly that. Daughters are blessed to be like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah.
Why these two boys, and not the great patriarchs?
One answer some teachers give: look at the brothers before them in Genesis. Cain and Abel, Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, Joseph and his brothers.
Then two brothers blessed in reverse order, and the text records no quarrel between them. Another answer: they grew up in Egypt, in a palace, and stayed who they were.
Genesis keeps choosing the younger. But in this scene, nobody loses. The younger one first, and the older one too.

how: On Friday night, before the Shabbat meal, many Jewish parents bless their children with hands on their heads: sons to be like Ephraim and Manasseh, daughters like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, followed by the priestly blessing.

o: and he blessed, Joseph's sons before Jacob
and he lived, the portion of Jacob's last days
the firstborn, the son who gets the right hand

games.q: who's who at the blessing — tap the pairs.
p: the younger, under the right hand
the firstborn, under the left hand
tried to move his father's hand
I know it, my son, I know it

s: Jacob crossed his hands by mistake, since he couldn't see well
the text says he guided his hands wittingly: on purpose. when Joseph objected, he said I know it.
Jacob said the older grandson would be great too
Manasseh, he said, would also become a people and also be great.
parents still bless sons to be like Ephraim and Manasseh
many Jewish families say it on Friday nights, as Jacob said they would.

games.q: you're Joseph. your father has crossed his hands and put the stronger blessing on your younger son. what do you do?
o: take his hand to move it to the firstborn.
games.why: Joseph tried to move the hand. Jacob refused: I know it, my son, I know it. and he blessed the older one to be great too.

practice: Picture a group you're part of, a family, a team, an office, a class, and the one who stands a little to the side: the newest person, the quiet one, the kid who's always second.
Then think of one small way to put a hand on their head, so to speak: a question just for them, or their name, said first for once.

wordCard.voice: Vayechi. The portion where the dying Jacob crosses his hands and blesses the younger grandson first, and the older one too.

orig.note: Hebrew: God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh. The blessing for sons (Genesis 48:20).

carryVoice: Your line: the younger one too. Parents still say it on Friday nights. Day two hundred eighteen.
